At 4:17 every morning, the town’s clocks stopped.

No one knew why. The church clock froze with its hands pointing at four and seventeen. The digital clock above the bakery displayed 4:17 in green, unblinking numbers. Even the clocks people kept in drawers, cupboards, glove compartments, and beside their beds surrendered to the same invisible command. Some stopped during the night. Others stopped in broad daylight, their hands shivering briefly before settling into place.

At first, people were frightened.

They called electricians, clockmakers, priests, engineers, and the sort of men who arrived in vans with ladders strapped to the roof. Batteries were replaced. Wires were examined. A scientist from the capital set up three cameras in the square and spent a week sleeping in his car. At 4:16 on the seventh morning, he stood beneath the clock tower, smiling triumphantly.

At 4:17, every camera stopped recording.

After that, people grew used to it.

The baker began waking at 4:17 and kneading dough by candlelight. The night watchman carried a pocket watch that he never bothered to wind. Children made games of shouting the time and throwing stones at the clock tower. Lovers began arranging to meet at 4:17, because it was the only time everyone could agree upon.

Then, one winter morning, a girl named Mara asked a question.

“What happens after?”

She was eight years old, with a missing front tooth and a habit of collecting things nobody else wanted: bottle caps, rusted nails, feathers, buttons, bones. Her mother told her that after 4:17 came 4:18, then 4:19, and so on, the way one step follows another.

“But where does 4:17 go?” Mara asked.

Her mother was standing at the sink, washing a blue cup.

“It doesn’t go anywhere.”

“Everything goes somewhere.”

“Not everything.”

Mara considered this. Outside, snow pressed its white face against the window. Across the street, the clock tower watched the town with its stopped hands.

That afternoon, Mara climbed the tower.

The door was locked, but locks were only puzzles, and puzzles were meant to be solved. She used a hairpin, a bent spoon, and finally the thin metal strip from an old umbrella. The stairs spiraled upward through dust and pigeon feathers. Halfway up, she found names carved into the wall: ELIAS, 1922; S. VALE, 1951; DON’T LOOK DOWN, 1978.

At the top, she entered the clock room.

The machinery was enormous. Brass gears stood taller than she did, teeth interlocked in solemn silence. Dust lay over everything except one small section near the center, where the metal shone brightly, as if touched every day.

Mara stepped closer.

There, between two gears, was a red thread.

It passed through the mechanism and disappeared into the wall.

She tugged it.

The entire tower shuddered.

Below, every clock in town began to tick.

Mara pulled harder.

The hands on the great clock moved. Not forward, but backward. 4:17 became 4:16, then 4:15. The bells began to ring, though no one had touched them. Their sound rolled over the rooftops, waking dogs, babies, and old men who had not slept properly in years.

Mara pulled until the thread came free.

Behind it, hidden in the wall, was a narrow door.

She opened it and found a room no larger than a closet. Inside stood a man.

He was very old. His hair was white, his coat was gray, and his face seemed familiar in the way dreams are familiar. He sat at a desk covered with clocks. Hundreds of them. Thousands, perhaps. Some were tiny as coins; others were large enough to fill a bathtub. None had hands.

The old man looked at Mara.

“You’re early,” he said.

“Early for what?”

“For the question.”

Mara held the red thread in both hands. “Where does 4:17 go?”

The old man smiled sadly.

“It comes here.”

He pointed to the clocks.

Mara walked among them. Each clock contained something different. In one, she saw a woman kissing a man on a railway platform. In another, a boy opened a letter and began to cry. One contained a summer field, bright with yellow flowers. One contained a kitchen where someone was laughing so hard they had to hold the table.

“These are memories,” Mara said.

“Not exactly.”

“Then what?”

“Moments that had nowhere else to go.”

The old man explained that every town had a lost minute. A minute when all the things people could not bear to lose were gathered and kept safe: last goodbyes, first breaths, doors that should have been opened, words that should have been spoken. The town’s 4:17 was made of these things.

“Who keeps them?” Mara asked.

“For a while, I did.”

“And now?”

He looked at her.

Mara understood.

“No,” she said.

The old man stood with difficulty. His knees cracked like branches. He took a small clock from the desk and placed it in her palm.

It had no hands, but it ticked.

“I don’t want to,” Mara said.

“Nobody does.”

“What happens if I refuse?”

“Then the moments spill out.”

“Is that bad?”

“Not always.”

Below them, the town was waking. The clock tower bells had stopped. Snow slid from the roofs in soft avalanches.

Mara thought of her mother at the sink. She thought of her father, who had left three years ago and never written. She thought of all the things she had collected because they seemed too lonely to leave behind.

“What do I have to do?” she asked.

The old man opened the door.

“Listen.”

Mara returned to the clock room. The red thread lay at her feet. She picked it up and tied it back between the gears. The machinery groaned, then settled.

At exactly 4:17, the town’s clocks stopped again.

But this time Mara heard something beneath the silence.

A thousand small sounds.

A train departing. A match struck in darkness. A baby breathing. Someone whispering, Stay. Someone else whispering, Go. A cup placed gently in a sink. A door closing. A door opening.

She listened until the sounds became one sound, and that sound became a heartbeat.

Years passed.

Mara grew tall. Her mother’s hair turned silver. The town changed its streets, its shops, and its names, but the clocks still stopped every morning at 4:17.

People said Mara was strange because she always knew when someone was about to leave. She could tell when a letter had been written but not sent. She could find lost keys, lost dogs, lost courage.

When she was old, she climbed the tower one final time.

The room behind the wall was waiting.

The old man was gone. The clocks remained.

Mara sat at the desk. She placed her hands upon it. For a moment, she felt the weight of every unfinished thing in the world.

Then the door opened below.

A little boy climbed the stairs.

He had a missing front tooth and pockets full of bottle caps.

“You’re early,” Mara told him.

“Early for what?”

“For the question.”

He looked at the red thread.

“Where does 4:17 go?”

Mara smiled and reached for his hand.

“It comes here,” she said.
